:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Personal versus regional inequality

Most inequality research asks how outcomes differ **between individuals**, and does not group people geographically. It never asks whether the differences follow a *pattern* — whether the disadvantaged are concentrated in one part of the map.

- we will take the regional view
- we will consider **time** as a first-class dimension. 
:::

:::{.callout-warning}
## Why is it important?

- causes of civil unrest
- political polarization
:::

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}

pci[["GeoName", "Region", "1969", "1993", "2017"]].head()

## Global inequality: the 20:20 ratio {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## The simplest robust measure

The income at the 80th percentile divided by the income at the 20th:

```{python}
r2020 = [pci[y].quantile(0.8) / pci[y].quantile(0.2) for y in years]

print(f"  1969 : {r2020[0]:.3f}")
print(f"  1990 : {r2020[21]:.3f}")
print(f"  2017 : {r2020[-1]:.3f}")
print(f"  peak : {max(r2020):.3f} in {years[int(numpy.argmax(r2020))]}")
```

In 1969 the richest 20% of counties had incomes **1.5×** the poorest 20%. Its virtue is robustness: it ignores both tails entirely, so a handful of extreme counties cannot move it.

Its vice is the same thing — it uses **two numbers** and discards the rest of the distribution.
:::

## Global inequality: the 20:20 ratio {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Graph over time
```{python}
#| code-fold: true
def ineq_20_20(values):
    top20, bottom20 = values.quantile([0.8, 0.2])
    return top20 / bottom20


# Generate range of strings from 1969 to 2018
years = numpy.arange(1969, 2018).astype(str)
# Compute 20:20 ratio for every year
ratio_2020 = pci[years].apply(ineq_20_20, axis=0)
# Plot evolution of 20:20 ratio
ax = plt.plot(years, ratio_2020)

# Grab figure generated in the plot
figure = plt.gcf()
# Replace tick labels with every other year
plt.xticks(years[::2])
# Set vertical label
plt.ylabel("20:20 ratio")
# Set horizontal label
plt.xlabel("Year")
# Rotate year labels
figure.autofmt_xdate(rotation=45)

plt.show()
```
:::

## The Lorenz curve {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## Cumulative share against cumulative population

Plot the cumulative share of income against the cumulative share of population, both sorted poorest-first. Perfect equality is the diagonal: $p$% of the population earning exactly $p$% of the income.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
f, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.4, 3.6))
n = len(pci)
share_pop = numpy.arange(1, n + 1) / n
for y, c in [("1969", "tab:blue"), ("2017", "tab:orange")]:
    v = numpy.sort(pci[y].values)
    ax.plot(share_pop, v.cumsum() / v.sum(), label=y, color=c)
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k--", lw=1, label="perfect equality")
ax.set_xlabel("cumulative share of counties")
ax.set_ylabel("cumulative share of income")
ax.legend(fontsize=7)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The **Gini index** is the area between the diagonal and the curve, divided by the area under the diagonal (which is always$\tfrac12$). 
:::

## The Gini index over time {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## One number per year

`inequality.gini.Gini` computes the coefficient for one year. Wrap it in a function and apply it across every year column:

```{python}
import inequality


def gini_by_col(column):
    return inequality.gini.Gini(column.values).g


inequalities = pci[years].apply(gini_by_col, axis=0).to_frame("gini")
inequalities.head()
```

`Gini` expects a NumPy array rather than a `pandas.Series`, hence `.values`.
:::

## The Gini index over time {.scrollable}

```{python}
inequalities.plot(figsize=(8, 3));
```

## Theil's index {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Definition

A third commonly used measure of inequality is Theil's $T$:

$$T = \sum_{i=1}^m \left( \frac{y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^m y_i} \ln \left[ m \frac{y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^m y_i}\right] \right)$$

where $y_i$ is per capita income in area $i$ among $m$ areas. Conceptually it is related to the **entropy** of the income distribution, measuring how evenly incomes are spread across the areas.
:::

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Reading the formula

Write $s_i = y_i / \sum_j y_j$ for area $i$'s **share** of total income. Under perfect equality every share would be $1/m$, so $m\,s_i$ is the area's share *relative to its equal share*:

- $m\,s_i > 1$ --- richer than equal, $\ln$ term positive
- $m\,s_i < 1$ --- poorer than equal, $\ln$ term negative

Each term is weighted by $s_i$ itself, so richer areas count for more --- which is why Theil is more sensitive to the **upper tail** than Gini.

:::

## Gini and Theil {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Two indices, computed the same way

```{python}
from inequality.gini import Gini
from inequality.theil import Theil

gini = [Gini(pci[y].values).g for y in years]
theil = [Theil(pci[y].values).T for y in years]

print(f"  Gini   1969 {gini[0]:.4f} -> 2017 {gini[-1]:.4f}   (peak {max(gini):.4f} in {years[int(numpy.argmax(gini))]})")
print(f"  Theil  1969 {theil[0]:.4f} -> 2017 {theil[-1]:.4f}")
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
f, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7, 2.6))
ax[0].plot(range(1969, 2018), gini); ax[0].set_title("Gini", fontsize=9)
ax[1].plot(range(1969, 2018), theil, color="tab:red"); ax[1].set_title("Theil", fontsize=9)
for a in ax: a.set_xlabel("year")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::

## Personal vs. regional income {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Setting up the notation

There is a subtle but important distinction between the study of **personal** and **regional** income inequality. To see it, express the two in one framework.

Consider a country of $N$ individuals distributed over $m$ regions.

- $Y_l$ --- the income of individual $l$
- $Y_i = \sum_{l \in i} Y_l$ --- total personal income in region $i$
- $N_i$ --- the number of individuals in region $i$
- $y_i = \dfrac{Y_i}{N_i}$ --- **per capita** income in region $i$
- $\bar{y}$ --- national per capita income, averaged over *people*, not over regions

Our data is the $y_i$.
:::

## Inequality between people {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Start from the national dispersion

At the national level, the **coefficient of variation** of individual incomes is a natural index of interpersonal inequality:

$$CV_{nat} = \frac{1}{\bar{y}}\sqrt{\frac{\sum_{l=1}^N (Y_l - \bar{y})^2}{N}}$$

The key component is the **total sum of squares**, and unpacking it sheds light on the personal-versus-regional question:

$$TSS = \sum_{l=1}^N (Y_l - \bar{y})^2$$
:::

## Inequality between people {.scrollable}
:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Split each person's deviation in two

An individual deviation $\delta_l = Y_l - \bar{y}$ is individual $l$'s contribution to inequality. It breaks exactly into two parts:

$$\delta_l = \underbrace{(Y_l - y_i)}_{\text{person vs their region}} + \underbrace{(y_i - \bar{y})}_{\text{region vs the nation}}$$

The first term is the difference between the individual's income and per capita income **in the region where they live**. The second is the difference between that region's per capita income and the national average.
:::

## The regional assumption {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-warning icon=false}
## We cannot see inside a region

In regional studies the intra-regional personal income distribution is typically **not available**. So the assumption is often made that intra-regional personal inequality is **zero**: everyone in the same region has the same income.

The first term then vanishes, $Y_l - y_i = 0$, and the total sum of squares collapses onto the regions:

$$
\begin{aligned}
TSS &= \sum_{l=1}^N (Y_l - \bar{y})^2 \\
    &= \sum_{l=1}^N \delta_l^2 \\
    &= \sum_{l=1}^N \big((Y_l - y_i) + (y_i - \bar{y})\big)^2 \\
    &= \sum_{l=1}^N \big(0 + (y_i - \bar{y})\big)^2 \\
    &= \sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{l \in i} (y_i - \bar{y})^2 \\
    &= \sum_{i=1}^m N_i\,(y_i - \bar{y})^2
\end{aligned}
$$

In the inner sums, $i$ means *the region individual $l$ lives in*.
:::

## What the assumption buys {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Inequality between places, not people

Under the assumption, each individual in region $i$ makes the **same** contribution to national inequality, a deviation of $(y_i - \bar{y})$. The region as a whole contributes $N_i(y_i - \bar{y})$ in deviations, and $N_i(y_i - \bar{y})^2$ to the sum of squares --- so **big regions far from the average dominate**.

The assumption may look overly restrictive, but it isolates the nature of **inter-regional** inequality: inequality *between places* rather than between people within them. In essence it shifts the question up one level of the spatial hierarchy, from individuals to areal units.
:::

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## The split is exact even without the assumption

Expand the square and the cross term disappears, because deviations from a region's own mean sum to zero within that region. So for **any** distribution of incomes:

$$TSS = \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{l \in i} (Y_l - y_i)^2}_{\text{within regions}} + \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^m N_i\,(y_i - \bar{y})^2}_{\text{between regions}}$$

The zero-inequality assumption does not create this split; it **deletes the first term**. Regional data measures the second term only, and says nothing about the first.
:::

## Inequality with a geography {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Is high income clustered, and is it becoming more so?

Neither Gini nor Theil knows where anything is — shuffle the counties across the map and both are unchanged. To bring geography in, return to Moran's $I$ from Geo 6 and compute it for **every year**.

```{python}
from libpysal import weights as W
from esda.moran import Moran

wq = W.Queen.from_dataframe(pci, use_index=False)
wq.transform = "r"
morans = [Moran(pci[y].values, wq).I for y in years]

for lbl, i in [("1969", 0), ("1993", 24), ("2017", -1)]:
    print(f"  {lbl} : Moran's I = {morans[i]:.4f}")
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
f, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 2.6))
ax.plot(range(1969, 2018), morans)
ax.set_xlabel("year"); ax.set_ylabel("Moran's $I$ of income")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::

## Reading that trend {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Spatial clustering of income has weakened steadily

$I$ falls from **0.649** to **0.421** — still strongly positive, and a steady decline: lower at every eight-year step (correlation with year −0.96), though not every single year --- it rises in 19 of 48.

Rich counties are still next to rich counties. But the map has become **less** organised by geography over fifty years: where you are predicts your income less well in 2017 than in 1969.

:::

<!-- source: gdsbook ch.9, "Regional decomposition of inequality" -->

## Regional decomposition of inequality {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Is inequality "explained" by groups?

A common objection to measuring inequality in aggregate: it says nothing about the **scale** at which inequality matters. Observed inequality can be driven by differences *between groups* rather than between similar individuals --- it can be "explained" by a confounding variable such as age, sex or education. Older people have had longer to gain experience and are generally paid more for it, so age alone accounts for a large part of the inequality in wealth.

So it is often useful to **decompose** an inequality index into groups: how much of it comes from differences between the groups, how much from differences inside them, and how unequal each group is on its own.

In geographic applications the groups are usually **regions** --- contiguous groups of observations (Shorrocks & Wan, 2005). Decomposing by region is a way of introducing geography into the study of inequality.
:::

## The regions {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Eight regions

The `Region` column assigns each county to one of eight regions:

```{python}
region_names = {
    1: "New England",
    2: "Mideast",
    3: "Great Lakes",
    4: "Plains",
    5: "Southeast",
    6: "Southwest",
    7: "Rocky Mountain",
    8: "Far West",
}
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
ax = pci.assign(Region_Name=pci.Region.map(region_names)).plot(
    "Region_Name",
    linewidth=0,
    legend=True,
    categorical=True,
    legend_kwds=dict(bbox_to_anchor=(1.3, 0.5), fontsize=7),
    figsize=(7, 4),
)
ax.set_axis_off();
```

These are the **Bureau of Economic Analysis** regions --- the income data itself is BEA table CAINC1. The book calls them Census Bureau regions; the Census Bureau's own scheme is 4 regions and 9 divisions.
:::

## Regional mean incomes {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Split, apply, combine

Group the counties by region, take the mean of every year column, and combine into one table --- a row per region, a column per year:

```{python}
rmeans = (
    pci.assign(Region_Name=pci.Region.map(region_names))
    .groupby(by="Region_Name")[years]
    .mean()
)
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
ax = rmeans.T.plot.line(figsize=(8, 3.6))
ax.set_ylabel("mean per capita income ($)")
ax.legend(fontsize=7, ncol=2);
```

These are **nominal** dollars, so the common upward trend is mostly inflation. What matters for inequality is the **spread between the lines**, and that is what the decomposition measures.
:::

## The decomposition, formally {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Theil's $T$ = between + within

Write the per capita incomes of the $m$ areas as $y = (y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_m)$, grouped into $\omega$ mutually exclusive regions. If $m_g$ is the number of areas in region $g$, then every area is counted exactly once:

$$\sum_{g=1}^{\omega} m_g = m$$

(This would fail if an area belonged to two regions and were counted twice.) Theil's index then splits into a between and a within part:

$$
\begin{aligned}
T &= \sum_{i=1}^m \left( \frac{y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^m y_i} \ln \left[ m \frac{y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^m y_i}\right] \right) \\
  &= \left[ \sum_{g=1}^{\omega} s_{g} \ln \left(\frac{m}{m_g} s_g \right)  \right] + \left[ \sum_{g=1}^{\omega} s_g \sum_{i \in g} s_{i,g} \ln \left(m_g s_{i,g}\right) \right] \\
  &= B + W
\end{aligned}
$$

where $s_g = \dfrac{\sum_{i \in g} y_i}{\sum_i y_i}$ is region $g$'s share of total income, and $s_{i,g} = y_i / \sum_{i \in g} y_i$ is area $i$'s share of its own region's income.
:::

## Computing the decomposition {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## `TheilD`

```{python}
theil_dr = inequality.theil.TheilD(pci[years].values, pci.Region)
```

The between and within components for every year are in the `bg` and `wg` attributes:

```{python}
theil_dr.bg[:5]
```

Store them alongside the earlier results, and compute the **share** of total inequality that is between regions:

```{python}
inequalities["theil"] = theil_dr.T
inequalities["theil_between"] = theil_dr.bg
inequalities["theil_within"] = theil_dr.wg
inequalities["theil_between_share"] = (
    inequalities["theil_between"] / inequalities["theil"]
)
inequalities[["theil", "theil_between", "theil_within", "theil_between_share"]].head()
```
:::

:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## Is the decomposition significant?

Inference uses `inequality.theil.TheilDSim`, which permutes the region labels across counties. The book omits it for brevity and reports that every decomposition is significant. Spot-checking 1969 and 2017 with 99 permutations, the between-region component sits at the permutation floor, $p = 0.01$, in both years.
:::

## Three series over time {.scrollable}

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
inequalities[
    ["theil_between", "theil_within", "theil_between_share"]
].plot(subplots=True, figsize=(8, 6));
```

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## What they show

The between-region **share** is lowest in the **mid-2000s** (11.7% in 2006), not the mid-1990s. Regional differences mattered a great deal in the 1970s and 1980s --- nearly a third of all county inequality in 1969 --- and their importance has waned relative to inequality **within** regions.
:::

<!-- source: gdsbook ch.9, "Spatializing classic measures" -->

## Spatializing classic measures {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## A region is just a group

Regional decompositions are useful, but they do not tell the whole story. A "region" is just a special kind of group: its geography shows up only through **membership** --- is the county *in* the region or not?

That kind of thinking is *place-based*, but not *spatial*. It never uses distance or proximity. Rearrange the regions on the map and, as long as membership is unchanged, every statistic is identical. (Shuffled regions are arguably no longer regions --- but the methods would not notice.)

The alternative is to build space **into** a classic measure. Rey & Smith (2012) do this for the Gini coefficient.
:::

## The Gini as pairwise differences {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Rewrite the Gini, then split it

The Gini can be written in terms of all pairwise absolute differences in income:

$$G = \frac{\sum_i \sum_j \left | y_i - y_j \right|}{2 n^2 \bar{y}}$$

where $n$ is the number of observations and $\bar{y}$ the mean income. Those pairs divide into **neighbouring** ones and **distant** ones:

$$
\sum_i \sum_j \left |y_i - y_j \right | = \sum_i \sum_j \underbrace{w_{ij} \left |y_i - y_j \right |}_{\text{near differences}} + \underbrace{(1-w_{ij})  \left |y_i - y_j \right |}_{\text{far differences}}
$$

where $w_{ij} = 1$ if $i$ and $j$ are neighbours and $0$ otherwise --- exactly a binary spatial weights matrix. So:

$$G = \underbrace{\frac{\sum_i \sum_j w_{ij}\left | y_i - y_j \right|}{2 n^2 \bar{y}}}_{\text{near: the spatial Gini}} + \underbrace{\frac{\sum_i \sum_j (1-w_{ij}) \left | y_i - y_j \right|}{2 n^2 \bar{y}}}_{\text{far}}$$

The **spatial Gini** is the first term. (Non-binary weights need a correction factor, not covered here.)
:::

## What the spatial Gini tells you {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Near against far

- **Strong positive spatial dependence** --- neighbours have similar incomes, so the near differences are small. Most of the inequality comes from disparities between *distant* places.
- **Weak (or negative) dependence** --- near differences are as large as anywhere else, and the two components equalise in proportion to the number of pairs in each.

Inference uses random spatial permutations of the income values: does the near component differ from what you would get with incomes scattered randomly over the map?
:::

:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## A complement to the Theil decomposition

Theil's regional decomposition never looks at **pairs** of observations; the spatial Gini is built from them. That makes it more sensitive --- and more easily moved by a small group of very wealthy places.
:::

## The spatial Gini for 1969 {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## `Gini_Spatial`

The spatial Gini needs **binary** weights, so switch the queen matrix back from row-standardised:

```{python}
from inequality.gini import Gini_Spatial

wq.transform = "B"
numpy.random.seed(12345)
gs69 = Gini_Spatial(pci["1969"], wq)

print(f"Gini (aspatial)       : {gs69.g:.4f}")
print(f"far component         : {gs69.wcg_share:.4f}")
print(f"far share of the Gini : {gs69.wcg_share / gs69.g:.2%}")
print(f"p_sim                 : {gs69.p_sim}")
```

The near component is significantly different from what random placement would give: inequality between neighbouring counties is not like inequality between distant ones.
:::

:::{.callout-warning icon=false}
## `wcg_share` is not a share

The book describes `wcg_share` as "the share of the overall Gini due to the far differences". In the library it is `wcg / (2n²ȳ)` --- the far **component**, in the same units as $G$ (0.1354 against $G$ = 0.1356). The share is that divided by $G$: **99.9%**.
:::

## Every year {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## The function-by-column pattern again

Return the Gini, the near and far components, and the pseudo $p$-value for each year:

```{python}
def gini_spatial_by_col(incomes, weights):
    gs = Gini_Spatial(incomes, weights)
    denom = 2 * incomes.mean() * weights.n ** 2
    near_diffs = gs.wg / denom
    far_diffs = gs.wcg / denom
    out = pandas.Series(
        {
            "gini": gs.g,
            "near_diffs": near_diffs,
            "far_diffs": far_diffs,
            "p_sim": gs.p_sim,
        }
    )
    return out


spatial_gini_results = pci[years].apply(gini_spatial_by_col, weights=wq).T.astype(float)
spatial_gini_results.head()
```

Inference is computationally demanding --- every permutation recomputes all the neighbour differences --- so this cell takes around 20 seconds.
:::

## Every year {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Always significant

```{python}
(spatial_gini_results.p_sim < 0.05).mean()
```

The $p$-value is below 0.05 in every year: the near component is always **smaller** than random placement would give. (A *larger* one would mean negative spatial dependence, which is rare in practice.)
:::

:::{.callout-warning icon=false}
## Read it with the pseudo $p$-value lesson from Geo 6

Every one of those $p$-values is exactly **0.01** --- the floor for 99 permutations. They do not say "$p = 0.01$"; they say "smaller than 99 permutations can resolve". More permutations would be needed to rank the years against each other.
:::

## Why the near component is so small {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Two reasons

**First, there are few neighbouring pairs.** Neighbours are less than 0.2% of all pairs of counties:

```{python}
wq.pct_nonzero
```

**Second, neighbours are similar** when spatial dependence is positive, so each near difference is small too. A small number of small differences adds up to very little.

The second reason can be measured. If neighbours were no more alike than any other pair, their share of all the absolute differences would equal their share of pairs:

```{python}
for y in ("1969", "2017"):
    gs = Gini_Spatial(pci[y], wq, permutations=0)
    print(f"  {y}: neighbours are {wq.s0 / (wq.n * (wq.n - 1)):.3%} of pairs "
          f"but carry {gs.wg / gs.dtotal:.3%} of the differences")
```

Neighbouring counties carry about **half** their fair share of the differences in 1969, rising toward **two-thirds** by 2017 --- neighbours became less alike.
:::

## Near differences and Moran's $I$ {.scrollable}

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
inequalities["near_diffs"] = spatial_gini_results.near_diffs
inequalities["I"] = morans

inequalities[["near_diffs", "I"]].plot.line(subplots=True, figsize=(8, 4.5));
```

```{python}
print(f"corr(near_diffs, Moran's I) = {inequalities['near_diffs'].corr(inequalities['I']):.3f}")
```

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Two views of one trend

As spatial dependence weakens --- Moran's $I$ falling --- the near differences grow. The spatial Gini and Moran's $I$ describe the same change from opposite sides: neighbouring counties have become **less alike** over fifty years.
:::

:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## Sources

- Shorrocks & Wan (2005), *Spatial decomposition of inequality*, **Journal of Economic Geography** 5(1). <https://doi.org/10.1093/jnlecg/lbh054>
- Rey & Smith (2012), *A spatial decomposition of the Gini coefficient*, **Letters in Spatial and Resource Sciences** 6. <https://doi.org/10.1007/s12076-012-0086-z>
:::
