# Clustering and regionalization

## Clusters {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Sorting observations without labels

Clustering borrows heavily from **unsupervised** statistical learning: observations are sorted into groups without any prior idea of what the groups are --- without labels.

Groups are delineated so that members of a group are **more similar to one another** than to members of other groups. Each group is a *cluster*; assigning observations to groups is *clustering*.

A good cluster can be characterised by its **profile** --- a simple summary of what its members are like across the original variables. Members may score consistently high on some traits and low on others, and the profile lets an analyst understand all of them at once instead of facing the full multivariate complexity.
:::

## Regions {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Clusters that are also places

A **region** is like a cluster: its members are grouped together and share a consistent profile. But a region also describes **a clear geographic area** --- its members must be geographically consistent.

Building regions is **regionalization**: clustering that groups observations similar in their attributes *and* in their location. It applies the logic of clustering plus a set of geographical constraints --- most often **connectivity**: two units can only be in the same region if a path joins them without leaving the region. Connectivity usually follows contiguity or proximity, though in some contexts it is relaxed or replaced by other constraints.
:::

:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## What follows

Using census data for San Diego tracts, we (1) explore the variables' statistical and spatial distributions, (2) build **geodemographic** clusters with k-means and Ward's hierarchical method, (3) see that those clusters are spatially **fragmented**, and (4) move to **regionalization**, which imposes geographic constraints.
:::

## Data {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## San Diego tracts, American Community Survey 2017

```{python}
from esda.moran import Moran
from libpysal.weights import Queen, KNN

db = geopandas.read_file(f"{GDS}/sandiego/sandiego_tracts.gpkg")
```

The variables used to characterise each tract:

```{python}
cluster_variables = [
    "median_house_value",  # Median house value
    "pct_white",  # % tract population that is white
    "pct_rented",  # % households that are rented
    "pct_hh_female",  # % female-led households
    "pct_bachelor",  # % tract population with a Bachelors degree
    "median_no_rooms",  # Median n. of rooms in the tract's households
    "income_gini",  # Gini index measuring tract wealth inequality
    "median_age",  # Median age of tract population
    "tt_work",  # Travel time to work
]
```
:::

## Each variable on its own {.scrollable}

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
f, axs = plt.subplots(nrows=3, ncols=3, figsize=(10, 10))
axs = axs.flatten()
for i, col in enumerate(cluster_variables):
    ax = axs[i]
    db.plot(column=col, ax=ax, scheme="Quantiles", linewidth=0, cmap="RdPu")
    ax.set_axis_off()
    ax.set_title(col)
plt.show()
```

:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## Reading the maps

Several variables increase from east to west (`pct_rented`, `median_house_value`, `median_no_rooms`, `tt_work`); others run the opposite way (`pct_white`, `pct_hh_female`, `pct_bachelor`, `median_age`).

That variety is what makes clustering useful: when variables have *different* spatial distributions, each contributes distinct information to the cluster profiles. If every map looked alike, there would be less information than it seems.
:::

## Spatial autocorrelation of each variable {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Moran's $I$, variable by variable

Spatial autocorrelation in the inputs shapes the spatial structure of the clusters. With queen contiguity weights:

```{python}
w = Queen.from_dataframe(db)

numpy.random.seed(123456)
mi_results = [Moran(db[variable], w) for variable in cluster_variables]
mi_results = [
    (variable, res.I, res.p_sim)
    for variable, res in zip(cluster_variables, mi_results)
]
table = pandas.DataFrame(
    mi_results, columns=["Variable", "Moran's I", "P-value"]
).set_index("Variable")
table
```

Every variable shows **significant positive** spatial autocorrelation: the clusters we find are likely to have a non-random spatial distribution.
:::

## How the variables relate {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## Moran's $I$ is one variable at a time

Autocorrelation says nothing about how attributes **co-vary**. Comparing all pairs of maps would mean 36 comparisons for 9 variables, so instead look at the pairwise relationships directly, without geography, in a scatterplot matrix:
:::

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
_ = seaborn.pairplot(db[cluster_variables], kind="reg", diag_kind="kde", height=1.3)
```

## Reading the scatterplot matrix {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Diagonal and off-diagonal

**Diagonal** --- each variable's density. Some are negatively skewed (`pct_white`, `pct_hh_female`), others positively skewed (`median_house_value`, `pct_bachelor`, `tt_work`).

**Off-diagonal** --- each pair's association. Some are positive (`median_age` vs `median_house_value`, `median_house_value` vs `median_no_rooms`), others negative (`median_house_value` vs `pct_rented`, `median_no_rooms` vs `pct_rented`, `median_age` vs `pct_rented`). `tt_work` is weakly associated with everything, partly because its values are so concentrated.
:::

## Distances depend on units {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Clustering is driven by distances between observations

Similarity is computed as the statistical *distance* between observations, and distances are sensitive to the units of measurement. Locate the first tracts by house price and Gini coefficient:

```{python}
db[["income_gini", "median_house_value"]].head()
```

```{python}
from sklearn import metrics

metrics.pairwise_distances(
    db[["income_gini", "median_house_value"]].head()
).round(4)
```

The distance between the first two tracts is driven almost entirely by the difference in house value (259 100 dollars) and ignores the difference in Gini (about 0.11). A change of a **single dollar** in house value is as large as the *maximum possible* difference in Gini. A clustering algorithm using this distance would pay a lot of attention to house value and almost none to inequality.
:::

## Standardising {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## As a rule, scale before clustering

`sklearn.preprocessing` offers the common methods:

- `scale()` subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation: $z = \dfrac{x_i - \bar{x}}{\sigma_x}$. The result has mean 0 and variance 1, but can still be skewed or bimodal, and outliers can distort the mean and variance.
- `robust_scale()` uses the median and the inter-quartile range instead: $z = \dfrac{x_i - \tilde{x}}{\lceil x \rceil_{75} - \lceil x \rceil_{25}}$, where $\lceil x \rceil_p$ is the $p$-th percentile.
- `minmax_scale()` maps each variable onto $[0, 1]$: $z = \dfrac{x - \min(x)}{\max(x - \min(x))}$.

`robust_scale()` or `scale()` suit most clustering problems. Non-linear transformations (log, Box-Cox) should come *before* scaling.

```{python}
from sklearn.preprocessing import robust_scale

db_scaled = robust_scale(db[cluster_variables])
```
:::

:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## The next step

Univariate and bivariate exploration is a good start. The next question --- do nearby dots in each scatterplot represent the *same* tracts? --- is exactly what clustering explores.
:::

## Geodemographic clusters {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Multivariate clustering of places

**Geodemographic analysis** is multivariate clustering where the observations are geographical areas. The output is nearly always **mapped**.

These methods build a known number of clusters $k$, much smaller than the number of observations, and give each a unique label. Mapping the labels, with the profiles in hand, shows the spatial distribution of socio-demographic traits.

The power of the approach: **statistical variation across many dimensions is compressed into one categorical variable** that can be shown on a single map. 
:::

## K-means {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Assign, update, repeat

K-means groups observations into a pre-specified number of clusters so that each observation is closer to the **mean of its own cluster** than to the mean of any other:

1. assign every observation a random label among $k$
2. compute each cluster's multivariate mean
3. reassign every observation to the cluster with the closest mean
4. repeat until no observation changes cluster

The number of clusters must be chosen in advance; in practice the right number is unknown. Here, $k = 5$:

```{python}
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=5)
numpy.random.seed(1234)
k5cls = kmeans.fit(db_scaled)
k5cls.labels_[:5]
```

The integer labels denote **membership only** --- the numerical differences between them are meaningless.
:::

## Spatial distribution of clusters {.scrollable}

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
db["k5cls"] = k5cls.labels_
f, ax = plt.subplots(1, figsize=(6, 6))
db.plot(column="k5cls", categorical=True, legend=True, linewidth=0, ax=ax)
ax.set_axis_off()
plt.show()
```

:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## One map from nine variables

Clumps of tracts with the same colour emerge --- Tobler's first law reflected in the multivariate clusters. But the irregular tracts mislead the eye: the large eastern polygons make it look as if most tracts fall in one cluster. Tract sizes and shapes differ too much to judge by eye alone.
:::

## Statistical analysis of the cluster map {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Cardinality, and land area

Count the tracts in each cluster:

```{python}
k5sizes = db.groupby("k5cls").size()
k5sizes
```

Two very large clusters (0, 1), one medium-sized (2) and two small ones (3, 4). Now compare with land area, dissolving each cluster into a single polygon:

```{python}
areas = db.dissolve(by="k5cls", aggfunc="sum")["area_sqm"]
areas
```
:::

## Tracts against land area {.scrollable}

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
area_tracts = pandas.DataFrame({"No. Tracts": k5sizes, "Area": areas})
area_tracts = area_tracts * 100 / area_tracts.sum()
ax = area_tracts.plot.bar(figsize=(6, 3))
ax.set_xlabel("Cluster labels")
ax.set_ylabel("Percentage by cluster");
```

```{python}
areas[1] / areas.sum()
```

:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## The map was half right

Cluster 1 covers **well over half** of the county's land area --- the visual impression was correct. But cluster 0 has about as many tracts, packed into a small area. The map hid that.
:::

## Cluster profiles {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Mean of each variable, per cluster

Profiles turn arbitrary labels into meaningful groups. Use the **unscaled** values, which are easier to interpret:

```{python}
k5means = db.groupby("k5cls")[cluster_variables].mean()
k5means.T.round(3)
```

Cluster 3 has the highest average `median_house_value` and the highest inequality (`income_gini`); cluster 0 is the youngest (`median_age`), with relatively few rooms per household (`median_no_rooms`).
:::

:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## Means hide detail

A fuller summary is available with `describe()` --- but it quickly becomes an unwieldy wall of numbers:

```python
# Illustrative code only, not executed
k5desc = db.groupby("k5cls")[cluster_variables].describe()
for cluster in k5desc.T:
    print("\n\t---------\n\tCluster %i" % cluster)
    print(k5desc.T[cluster].unstack())
```
:::

## Distributional profiles {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Tidy the data, then plot distributions

A better profile draws each cluster's **distribution** for every variable. First reshape to a *tidy* (long) table --- one row per observation-variable pair:

```{python}
tidy_db = db.set_index("k5cls")
tidy_db = tidy_db[cluster_variables]
tidy_db = tidy_db.stack()
tidy_db = tidy_db.reset_index()
tidy_db = tidy_db.rename(columns={"level_1": "Attribute", 0: "Values"})
tidy_db.head()
```
:::

## Distributional profiles {.scrollable}

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
facets = seaborn.FacetGrid(
    data=tidy_db, col="Attribute", hue="k5cls",
    sharey=False, sharex=False, aspect=2, col_wrap=3, height=1.6,
)
_ = facets.map(seaborn.kdeplot, "Values", fill=True).add_legend()
```

:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## Reading the facets

Some attributes, such as the share of female-led households (`pct_hh_female`), have much the same distribution in every cluster. Others, such as `median_house_value`, separate the clusters clearly. Together, the panels show the multi-dimensional character of each cluster.
:::

## Hierarchical clustering {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Agglomerative hierarchical clustering (AHC)

AHC builds a **hierarchy** of solutions, from every observation as its own cluster to all observations in one. The extremes are useless; the solutions in between have varying levels of detail.

1. begin with every observation as its own cluster
2. find the two closest clusters by some distance metric
3. join them into a new cluster
4. repeat 2--3 until the desired level of aggregation

Like k-means, AHC needs the number of clusters specified, since the hierarchy contains every $k$ from $n$ down to 1.
:::

## AHC in code {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Ward's linkage, five clusters

```{python}
from sklearn.cluster import AgglomerativeClustering

numpy.random.seed(0)
model = AgglomerativeClustering(linkage="ward", n_clusters=5)
model.fit(db_scaled)
db["ward5"] = model.labels_
```

```{python}
ward5sizes = db.groupby("ward5").size()
ward5sizes
```

```{python}
ward5means = db.groupby("ward5")[cluster_variables].mean()
ward5means.T.round(3)
```
:::

## AHC profiles {.scrollable}

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
tidy_db = db.set_index("ward5")
tidy_db = tidy_db[cluster_variables]
tidy_db = tidy_db.stack()
tidy_db = tidy_db.reset_index()
tidy_db = tidy_db.rename(columns={"level_1": "Attribute", 0: "Values"})
facets = seaborn.FacetGrid(
    data=tidy_db, col="Attribute", hue="ward5",
    sharey=False, sharex=False, aspect=2, col_wrap=3, height=1.6,
)
facets.map(seaborn.kdeplot, "Values", fill=True).add_legend();
```

The interpretation is analogous to that of the k-means profiles.

## K-means and AHC on the map {.scrollable}

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
f, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 5))
db.plot(column="k5cls", categorical=True, cmap="Set2", legend=True, linewidth=0, ax=axs[0])
axs[0].set_axis_off()
axs[0].set_title("K-Means solution ($k=5$)")
db.plot(column="ward5", categorical=True, cmap="Set3", legend=True, linewidth=0, ax=axs[1])
axs[1].set_axis_off()
axs[1].set_title("AHC solution ($k=5$)")
plt.show()
```

:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## Similar structure, fragmented clusters

The two solutions are not identical, but they capture very similar overall spatial structure. And both slightly violate Tobler's law: every cluster has **disconnected components**. Each of the five clusters is made of many separate areas, strewn around the map by the structure of the data, not its geography --- to visit every tract in a cluster you would have to pass through other clusters.
:::

## Regionalization {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## When clusters must be connected

Fragmented clusters are not invalid --- particularly for exploring the overall structure of multivariate data. But some applications need every member of a class to be **spatially connected**: communities, neighbourhoods, electoral or census boundaries are nearly always self-connected areas.

**Regionalization** methods are clustering techniques with a **spatial constraint**: their output clusters are internally connected, so a region's members are *nested* within its boundary.

Real-world nestings exist --- counties within US states, LSOAs within MSOAs in the UK --- but those are aggregated by *administrative* principles. A regionalization aggregates by **statistical similarity**, under the constraint.
:::

## The contiguity constraint {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## AHC, allowed to merge only neighbours

```{python}
numpy.random.seed(123456)
model = AgglomerativeClustering(linkage="ward", connectivity=w.sparse, n_clusters=5)
model.fit(db_scaled)
db["ward5wq"] = model.labels_
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
f, ax = plt.subplots(1, figsize=(6, 6))
db.plot(column="ward5wq", categorical=True, legend=True, linewidth=0, ax=ax)
ax.set_axis_off()
plt.show()
```

The clusters are now **fully connected**, with much more concentrated spatial distributions. Some tracts may look detached from their region, but each is joined to another member through a very narrow shared boundary.
:::

## Changing the spatial constraint {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## The weights define the constraint

The constraint is whatever the weights matrix says. Replace queen contiguity with each tract's **four nearest** tracts:

```{python}
w = KNN.from_dataframe(db, k=4)

numpy.random.seed(123456)
model = AgglomerativeClustering(linkage="ward", connectivity=w.sparse, n_clusters=5)
model.fit(db_scaled)
db["ward5wknn"] = model.labels_
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
f, ax = plt.subplots(1, figsize=(6, 6))
db.plot(column="ward5wknn", categorical=True, legend=True, linewidth=0, ax=ax)
ax.set_axis_off()
plt.show()
```
:::

## Which regionalization is "better"? {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Two kinds of coherence

Regionalizations are usually compared on:

- **geographical coherence** --- the *shape* of the regions. Are they evenly sized? Compact, or strangely shaped?
- **feature coherence** --- are observations more similar to their own cluster than to others? This *goodness of fit* is usually **better for unconstrained clustering** than for the corresponding regionalization.
:::

## Geographical coherence {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## The isoperimetric quotient

Compare a region's area with the area of a circle that has the **same perimeter**. The circle's circumference equals the region's perimeter, $P_i = 2\pi r_c$, so its area is $A_c = \pi r_c^2 = \pi \left(\frac{P_i}{2\pi}\right)^2$, and:

$$IPQ_i = \frac{A_i}{A_c} = \frac{4\pi A_i}{P_i^2}$$

Compact shapes have an IPQ near 1; elongated or spindly ones near 0. Clusters should score very low, since a cluster's perimeter shrinks the more boundaries its members share.

```{python}
results = []
for cluster_type in ("k5cls", "ward5", "ward5wq", "ward5wknn"):
    regions = db[[cluster_type, "geometry"]].dissolve(by=cluster_type)
    ipqs = regions.area * 4 * numpy.pi / (regions.boundary.length ** 2)
    result = ipqs.to_frame(cluster_type)
    results.append(result)
pandas.concat(results, axis=1)
```

The regionalizations' shapes are far more compact than the clusters'. The two regionalizations are broadly comparable to each other; in each, the highest value belongs to a region of a single tract, which is compact by itself. Many other shape measures live in `esda.shapestats`.
:::

## Feature coherence {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Goodness of fit

`sklearn.metrics` provides fit statistics, for example:

- `calinski_harabasz_score()` (CH) --- the ratio of between-cluster to within-cluster dispersion
- `silhouette_score()` --- the average standardised distance from each observation to its "next best" cluster

```{python}
ch_scores = []
for cluster_type in ("k5cls", "ward5", "ward5wq", "ward5wknn"):
    ch_score = metrics.calinski_harabasz_score(
        robust_scale(db[cluster_variables]),
        db[cluster_type],
    )
    ch_scores.append((cluster_type, ch_score))
pandas.DataFrame(ch_scores, columns=["cluster type", "CH score"]).set_index("cluster type")
```

For `metrics` functions ending in `score`, higher is better. K-means fits best, Ward second, and both regionalizations come **well below**: improved geographical coherence costs a lot of feature fit. A constrained solution mathematically *cannot* beat the unconstrained k-means solution, unless that solution happens to be a valid regionalization.
:::

## Solution similarity {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## How alike are the labellings?

`metrics` also compares labellings directly --- here with the adjusted mutual information score:

```{python}
ami_scores = []
for i_cluster_type in ("k5cls", "ward5", "ward5wq", "ward5wknn"):
    for j_cluster_type in ("k5cls", "ward5", "ward5wq", "ward5wknn"):
        ami_score = metrics.adjusted_mutual_info_score(
            db[i_cluster_type], db[j_cluster_type]
        )
        ami_scores.append((i_cluster_type, j_cluster_type, ami_score))
results = pandas.DataFrame(ami_scores, columns=["source", "target", "similarity"])
results.pivot(columns="source", index="target", values="similarity")
```

The regionalizations are generally **not** very similar to the clusterings, as expected. In this run the two regionalizations are the most similar pair --- more alike than k-means and Ward are to each other.
:::

# Spatial regression

## What is spatial regression? {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Two ways space helps a regression

**The process is explicitly spatial.** People pay a premium to live in a better school district; homes near noisy or polluting facilities sell for less; asthma incidence may depend more on where people *work and travel* than where they live. Here **geography is a feature**: it predicts because the outcome comes from geographical processes.

**Geography as a diagnostic.** We often care about what a model gets *wrong*. Mapping prediction errors shows whether there are **clusters of error** --- whether the model systematically mis-predicts some areas, or error is "contagious" between nearby observations. If so, that structure can be exploited to make better predictions.
:::

## Spatial structure in errors {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## Three sources

- geography *should* be an attribute, but we are not sure exactly how to include it
- some **other feature** whose omission causes the spatial pattern --- including it would make the structure disappear
- interactions among the predictors we chose: most social-science predictors carry **embodied spatial information**, so using spatially patterned predictors can produce spatially patterned errors, and using several can amplify the effect

So **whether or not the true process is explicitly geographic**, information about spatial relationships or about nearby sites can improve predictions.
:::

## Data: San Diego Airbnb {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Listings and their characteristics

```{python}
import spreg
from libpysal import weights
import esda

db = geopandas.read_file(f"{GDS}/airbnb/regression_db.geojson")
```

The table mixes intrinsic characteristics, both continuous (e.g. `beds`) and categorical (room type and property group binaries, `rt_X` and `pg_X`), with explicitly spatial variables such as distance to Balboa Park (`d2balboa`) and neighbourhood (`neighborhood`). The explanatory variables:

```{python}
variable_names = [
    "accommodates",  # Number of people it accommodates
    "bathrooms",  # Number of bathrooms
    "bedrooms",  # Number of bedrooms
    "beds",  # Number of beds
    # Below are binary variables, 1 True, 0 False
    "rt_Private_room",  # Room type: private room
    "rt_Shared_room",  # Room type: shared room
    "pg_Condominium",  # Property group: condo
    "pg_House",  # Property group: house
    "pg_Other",  # Property group: other
    "pg_Townhouse",  # Property group: townhouse
]
```
:::

## Non-spatial regression {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Explain one variable with others

Linear regression explains the variation in a *dependent* variable as a linear function of *explanatory* variables. At the individual level:

$$P_i = \alpha + \sum_k \mathbf{X}_{ik}\beta_k + \epsilon_i$$

where $P_i$ is the price of house $i$, $\mathbf{X}$ the covariates, $\beta$ the parameters, $\alpha$ the constant, and $\epsilon_i$ the error --- everything that influences price but is not in $\mathbf{X}$. In matrix form:

$$P = \alpha + \mathbf{X}\beta + \epsilon$$

Each $\beta_k$ is the association between variable $k$ and the dependent variable **keeping all other explanatory variables constant**. Regression isolates the distinct effect of one variable once we *control* for the others --- but only the confounders we include, not all of them.
:::

## Fitting it with `spreg` {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Ordinary least squares

`spreg` is used because it is the library that later lets us move into explicitly spatial econometric models. We model the **log** of the price, so results read as percentage changes:

```{python}
m1 = spreg.OLS(
    db[["log_price"]].values,
    db[variable_names].values,
    name_y="log_price",
    name_x=variable_names,
)
print(m1.summary)
```
:::

## Reading the coefficients {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## Largely as expected

Houses are significantly more expensive if they accommodate more people, have more bathrooms and bedrooms, or are a condominium or of the "other" type. Given the number of rooms, houses with more **beds** --- more crowded listings --- go for cheaper, as do private rooms and shared rooms rather than whole properties.

One might doubt that the number of beds can change *arbitrarily* without changing how many people a listing accommodates; interaction effects address this, but are not covered here.
:::

## Hidden structures {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## The errors may cluster

The model explains about two-thirds of the variation in log price ($R^2 \approx 0.67$). But clustering in the errors would violate the **i.i.d.** assumption linear models rely on.

A first check: the model knows nothing about **beaches**, which matter a lot in San Diego. Compare the residuals of coastal and non-coastal listings:

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
is_coastal = db.coastal.astype(bool)
coastal = m1.u[is_coastal]
not_coastal = m1.u[~is_coastal]
plt.hist(coastal, density=True, label="Coastal")
plt.hist(not_coastal, histtype="step", density=True, linewidth=4, label="Not Coastal")
plt.vlines(0, 0, 1, linestyle=":", color="k", linewidth=4)
plt.legend()
plt.show()
```
:::

## Coastal residuals {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## A $t$-test

Coastal neighbourhoods have only slightly higher average errors, with lower variance, but the two distributions are significantly different:

```{python}
from scipy.stats import ttest_ind

ttest_ind(coastal, not_coastal)
```

More sophisticated, harder-to-fool tests exist (the book's challenge questions explore one).
:::

## Residuals by neighbourhood {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Some neighbourhoods are systematically mis-predicted

Unmodelled preferences or marketing may make some neighbourhoods more desirable --- or less, as near the Camp Pendleton Marine base, despite being near the sea. Sort neighbourhoods by their median residual and look at the full distribution in each:

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
db["residual"] = m1.u
medians = db.groupby("neighborhood").residual.median().to_frame("hood_residual")
f = plt.figure(figsize=(11, 3))
ax = plt.gca()
seaborn.boxplot(
    x="neighborhood", y="residual", ax=ax,
    data=db.merge(medians, how="left", left_on="neighborhood", right_index=True)
    .sort_values("hood_residual"),
    palette="bwr",
)
f.autofmt_xdate(rotation=-90)
plt.show()
```

No neighbourhood is disjoint from the others, but some sit clearly higher --- the downtown tourist areas such as the Gaslamp Quarter, Little Italy and The Core. Neighbourhood "fashionableness" may matter in ways the model misses.
:::

## Contagion in the errors {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Each residual against its neighbour's

Many of the most over- and under-predicted neighbourhoods are near each other. Hosts pricing against nearby listings would produce **spillovers** the model cannot see. Using a $k$-nearest-neighbour weights matrix with $k = 1$, the spatial lag of the residual is simply the residual of the closest listing:

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
knn = weights.KNN.from_dataframe(db, k=1)
lag_residual = weights.spatial_lag.lag_spatial(knn, m1.u)
ax = seaborn.regplot(
    x=m1.u.flatten(), y=lag_residual.flatten(),
    line_kws=dict(color="orangered"), ci=None,
)
ax.set_xlabel("Model Residuals - $u$")
ax.set_ylabel("Spatial Lag of Model Residuals - $W u$");
```

Prediction errors cluster: when the model over-predicts a listing, it tends to over-predict its neighbours too. The relationship stabilises as the number of neighbours used grows.
:::

## Clusters of error {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Local Moran's $I_i$ on the residuals

With a stable $k = 20$, the local Moran statistics of Geo 6 locate significant clusters of model error:

```{python}
knn.reweight(k=20, inplace=True)
knn.transform = "R"
outliers = esda.moran.Moran_Local(m1.u, knn, permutations=9999)
error_clusters = outliers.q % 2 == 1
error_clusters &= outliers.p_sim <= 0.001
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
ax = (
    db.assign(error_clusters=error_clusters, local_I=outliers.Is)
    .query("error_clusters")
    .sort_values("local_I")
    .plot("local_I", cmap="bwr", marker=".")
)
contextily.add_basemap(ax, crs=db.crs, source=BASEMAP)
ax.set_axis_off();
```

These are places where the model significantly mis-predicts both a listing and its surroundings. If those areas have a **consistent geography** we can model, predictions can improve --- or at least stop being systematically wrong in some places.
:::

## Adding space {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Space as process, or space as proxy

Spatial regression introduces space *explicitly* into the regression framework

When?

- space plays a role in the process, e.g. seafront houses cost more than the second row, for the view 
- space can **proxy** for factors we should but cannot include, such as the "character" of a neighbourhood, hard to measure but easier to locate.

Processes giving rise to spatial effects:

- **spatial heterogeneity** 
- **spatial dependence**
- **independent variables**: leave the model unchanged 
:::

## Proximity variables {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Distance to Balboa Park

Balboa Park, with its museums and the San Diego Zoo, is a hub for visitors, who may pay a premium to stay near it. Omitting that would leave a **spatially patterned omitted covariate**. The distance itself:

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
ax = db.plot("d2balboa", marker=".", s=5)
contextily.add_basemap(ax, crs=db.crs, source=BASEMAP)
ax.set_axis_off();
```

Add it to the model:

```{python}
balboa_names = variable_names + ["d2balboa"]
m2 = spreg.OLS(
    db[["log_price"]].values,
    db[balboa_names].values,
    name_y="log_price",
    name_x=balboa_names,
)
pandas.DataFrame(
    [[m1.r2, m1.ar2], [m2.r2, m2.ar2]],
    index=["M1", "M2"],
    columns=["R2", "Adj. R2"],
)
```
:::

## Does distance to the park help? {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Not much

```{python}
pandas.DataFrame(
    {
        "Coeff.": m2.betas.flatten(),
        "Std. Error": m2.std_err.flatten(),
        "P-Value": [i[1] for i in m2.t_stat],
    },
    index=m2.name_x,
)
```

The coefficient is not significant at conventional levels and the fit barely changes. The errors still show spatial structure:

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
lag_residual = weights.spatial_lag.lag_spatial(knn, m2.u)
ax = seaborn.regplot(
    x=m2.u.flatten(), y=lag_residual.flatten(),
    line_kws=dict(color="orangered"), ci=None,
)
ax.set_xlabel("Residuals ($u$)")
ax.set_ylabel("Spatial lag of residuals ($Wu$)");
```

And the estimate is *positive*: people would be paying a premium to be **further** from the park, against our theory. Spatial heterogeneity, next, sheds some light on this.
:::

## Intercept and slopes {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## The two kinds of parameter

In the regression from earlier,

$$\log P_i = \alpha + \sum_k \mathbf{X}_{ik}\beta_k + \epsilon_i$$

- the **intercept** $\alpha$ is the predicted log price when every explanatory variable is zero --- the **baseline level** the other effects add to. Graphically, where the line crosses the vertical axis.
- each **slope** $\beta_k$ is the change in log price when $X_k$ rises by one unit, all other variables held fixed. Graphically, the steepness of the line. With a log outcome it reads as a **percentage change**, $e^{\beta_k} - 1$.

From the baseline model `m1`:

```{python}
b = dict(zip(m1.name_x, m1.betas.flatten()))
print(f"intercept : {b['CONSTANT']:.3f}  -> baseline price about ${numpy.exp(b['CONSTANT']):.0f}")
print(f"bedrooms  : {b['bedrooms']:.4f} -> each extra bedroom adds about {numpy.exp(b['bedrooms']) - 1:.1%}")
```
:::

:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## What spatial heterogeneity lets vary

- **Varying intercept** --- each place gets its own baseline level, but every variable has the same effect everywhere: parallel lines at different heights. These are **spatial fixed effects**.
- **Varying slopes** --- the *effect* of a variable differs by place: lines of different steepness. These are **spatial regimes**, whose coastal and inland estimates follow in a few slides.
:::

## Spatial heterogeneity {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Parts of the model vary across space

Not all neighbourhoods have the same prices: some are systematically more expensive regardless of distance to the park.

That is **spatial heterogeneity**: parts of the model change from place to place.

- variation in the **intercept** $\alpha$ --- different baseline exposure to the process
- variation in the **slopes** $\beta$ --- a geographic factor mediating a relationship, such as a policy applied unevenly across jurisdictions
- variation in the **error variance** $\sigma^2$ --- spatial heteroskedasticity
:::

## Spatial fixed effects {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Let $\alpha$ vary by neighbourhood

Geographic variation in $\alpha$ is called **spatial fixed effects** (FE) --- "space as a proxy". We are probably missing factors that determine price, and some vary systematically over space. We can control for them with binary variables built on a spatial rule: one per neighbourhood.

$$\log{P_i} = \alpha_r + \sum_k \mathbf{X}_{ik}\beta_k + \epsilon_i$$

With `statsmodels`' formula interface:

```{python}
import statsmodels.formula.api as sm

f = "log_price ~ " + " + ".join(variable_names) + " + neighborhood - 1"
print(f)
```

The trailing `- 1` drops the intercept: an intercept *plus* a unique mean for every neighbourhood would make the system of equations underspecified.

```{python}
m3 = sm.ols(f, data=db).fit()
```
:::

## The fixed effects {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## One coefficient per neighbourhood

```{python}
sfe_names = [i for i in m3.params.index if "neighborhood[" in i]
pandas.DataFrame(
    {
        "Coef.": m3.params[sfe_names],
        "Std. Error": m3.bse[sfe_names],
        "P-Value": m3.pvalues[sfe_names],
    }
)
```

Spatial FE are a regression with a categorical variable, modelled with binary dummies that `statsmodels` builds from the formula.
:::

## Fixed effects with `spreg` {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## The same model as a regime model

`spreg`'s *regimes* generalise fixed effects. Allowing only the constant to vary gives the FE model:

```{python}
m4 = spreg.OLS_Regimes(
    db[["log_price"]].values,
    db[variable_names].values,
    db["neighborhood"].tolist(),
    constant_regi="many",
    cols2regi=[False] * len(variable_names),
    regime_err_sep=False,
    name_y="log_price",
    name_x=variable_names,
)
numpy.round(m4.betas.flatten() - m3.params.values, decimals=12)
```

Identical to `statsmodels` to the 12th decimal.
:::

:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## What fixed effects do econometrically

Instead of comparing all prices across San Diego as equal, the model derives variation only from **within each neighbourhood**: each $\beta_k$ now compares only houses in the same area. Unobserved effects that align with the neighbourhoods are controlled for, isolating the variables' effects more cleanly.
:::

## Mapping the fixed effects {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## From coefficients to a map

Extract the neighbourhood effects and clean their names:

```{python}
neighborhood_effects = m3.params.filter(like="neighborhood")
stripped = neighborhood_effects.index.str.strip("neighborhood[").str.strip("]")
neighborhood_effects.index = stripped
neighborhood_effects = neighborhood_effects.to_frame("fixed_effect")
neighborhood_effects.head()
```

Then join them to the neighbourhood boundaries:

```{python}
neighborhoods = geopandas.read_file(f"{GDS}/airbnb/neighbourhoods.geojson")
```
:::

## Mapping the fixed effects {.scrollable}

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
ax = neighborhoods.plot(color="k", linewidth=0, alpha=0.5, figsize=(9, 5))
neighborhoods.merge(
    neighborhood_effects, how="left", left_on="neighbourhood", right_index=True
).dropna(subset=["fixed_effect"]).plot(
    "fixed_effect", scheme="quantiles", k=7, linewidth=0.1, cmap="viridis", ax=ax,
)
contextily.add_basemap(
    ax, crs=neighborhoods.crs, source=_carto(contextily.providers.CartoDB.PositronNoLabels)
)
ax.set_axis_off()
plt.show()
```

A clear spatial structure: the most expensive neighbourhoods tend to lie near the **coast**, the cheapest inland.

## Spatial regimes {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Let the slopes vary too

Fixed effects let only the constant vary geographically; everything else applies uniformly across space. **Spatial regimes** generalise this to any explanatory variable:

$$\log{P_i} = \alpha_r + \sum_k \mathbf{X}_{ki}\beta_{k-r} + \epsilon_i$$

Regimes here are defined by whether a listing is in a **coastal** neighbourhood: the pull of the ocean might be strong enough that people pay different *rates* for each characteristic of a house.

```{python}
m5 = spreg.OLS_Regimes(
    db[["log_price"]].values,
    db[variable_names].values,
    db["coastal"].tolist(),
    constant_regi="many",
    regime_err_sep=False,
    name_y="log_price",
    name_x=variable_names,
)
```
:::

## Regimes side by side {.scrollable}

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
res = pandas.DataFrame(
    {
        "Coeff.": m5.betas.flatten(),
        "Std. Error": m5.std_err.flatten(),
        "P-Value": [i[1] for i in m5.t_stat],
    },
    index=m5.name_x,
)
coastal = [i for i in res.index if "1_" in i]
coastal = res.loc[coastal, :].rename(lambda i: i.replace("1_", ""))
coastal.columns = pandas.MultiIndex.from_product([["Coastal"], coastal.columns])
ncoastal = [i for i in res.index if "0_" in i]
ncoastal = res.loc[ncoastal, :].rename(lambda i: i.replace("0_", ""))
ncoastal.columns = pandas.MultiIndex.from_product([["Non-coastal"], ncoastal.columns])
pandas.concat([coastal, ncoastal], axis=1).round(4)
```

The parameters mostly conform to expectations in both regimes.

## Do the regimes differ? {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## The Chow test

The Chow test's null hypothesis is that estimates from different regimes are indistinguishable. The global test, jointly over all coefficients (statistic, $p$-value):

```{python}
m5.chow.joint
```

The two regimes are statistically different. Variable by variable:

```{python}
pandas.DataFrame(
    m5.chow.regi,
    index=m5.name_x_r,
    columns=["Statistic", "P-value"],
)
```

Most variables do differ across regimes, pointing to systematic differences in the data-generating process between coastal and inland listings.
:::

## Spatial dependence {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## The configuration of observations

Spatial heterogeneity concerns effects *explicitly linked to geography*. **Spatial dependence** concerns the **spatial arrangement** of the observations themselves.

A house's price may depend not only on whether it is a townhouse or an apartment, but also on whether it is *surrounded* by townhouses or by high-rise apartments --- the "look and feel" of low-rise historic streets versus modern towers. That relates to the characteristics of the observations and how they are arranged, not to inherent features of the place.

Spatial dependence enters a regression through **spatial weights matrices** $\mathbf{W}$. Three ways follow, from the least invasive --- changing only the independent variables --- to substantial modifications of the model.
:::

## Exogenous effects: the SLX model {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Add the spatial lags of the explanatory variables

Renters may care about the houses *around* a listing, not only the listing. Include, besides each property-type dummy (`pg_XXX`), its spatial lag --- the **share of neighbouring houses of each type**:

$$\log(P_i) = \alpha + \sum^{p}_{k=1}X_{ij}\beta_j + \sum^{p}_{k=1}\left(\sum^{N}_{j=1}w_{ij}x_{jk}\right)\gamma_k + \epsilon_i$$

or, in matrix form:

$$\log(P_i) = \alpha + \mathbf{X}\beta + \mathbf{WX}\gamma + \epsilon$$

:::

## Reading $\beta$ and $\gamma$ {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## Direct and indirect effects

- **$\beta$** - the change in $y_i$ when $X_{ik}$ changes by one. Since the outcome is log price, $\beta$ reads as a **percentage** change. The subscript $i$ matters: with $\mathbf{W}$ involved, *where* the change happens matters.
- **$\gamma$** - the *indirect* association: the change in a house's price when its **average surroundings** change by one.

But a change at site $i$ **spills over**: when $x_i$ changes, so does the spatial lag of every site near $i$, by an amount that depends on $\mathbf{W}$. A highly connected site barely notices one neighbour changing; a site with one neighbour sees its lag change by exactly that neighbour's change. Finding the indirect effect of a change at a specific site means computing the **change in the spatial lag** and using that as the change in $X$.
:::

## The SLX model in code {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Lag every `pg_` variable

```{python}
wx = (
    db.filter(like="pg_")
    .apply(lambda y: weights.spatial_lag.lag_spatial(knn, y))
    .rename(columns=lambda c: "w_" + c)
    .drop("w_pg_Apartment", axis=1)
)
```

The lags are effectively additional exogenous variables, so OLS still applies:

```{python}
slx_exog = db[variable_names].join(wx)
m6 = spreg.OLS(
    db[["log_price"]].values,
    slx_exog.values,
    name_y="l_price",
    name_x=slx_exog.columns.tolist(),
)
```
:::

## SLX results {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## The property types and their lags

```{python}
vars_of_interest = db[variable_names].filter(like="pg_").join(wx).columns
pandas.DataFrame(
    {
        "Coeff.": m6.betas.flatten(),
        "Std. Error": m6.std_err.flatten(),
        "P-Value": [i[1] for i in m6.t_stat],
    },
    index=m6.name_x,
).reindex(vars_of_interest).round(4)
```

The spatial lags `w_pg_XXX` are the new additions, and all are significant at the 5% level --- the surrounding houses do seem to matter.
:::

:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## Interpreting them

**Direct:** condominiums are about **11%** more expensive than the benchmark, apartments ($\beta_{pg\_Condominium} = 0.1063$).

**Indirect:** a house surrounded by condominiums *also* gets a premium. Because `pg_Condominium` is a dummy, its spatial lag is the **share** of nearby properties that are condominiums, between 0 and 1. A 0.1 increase --- ten percentage points --- raises price by about **5.9%** ($\gamma_{w\_pg\_Condominium} \approx 0.59$). With a row-standardised 20-nearest-neighbour matrix, changing one site's $x_i$ changes each neighbour's lag by $1/20$, so the effect on each neighbour is $\gamma / 20 \approx 0.0296$. With other weights (Kernel, Queen, Rook, DistanceBand, Voronoi) the number of neighbours varies, and so would the effect.
:::

## Direct and indirect effects, by scenario {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Turn one apartment into a condominium

Predicted values live in the `predy` attribute of any `spreg` model:

```{python}
m6.predy[:3]
```

The third observation is an apartment. Copy the data and switch it to a condominium:

```{python}
db.loc[2, "pg_Apartment":"pg_Townhouse"]
```

```{python}
db_scenario = db.copy()
db_scenario.loc[2, ["pg_Apartment", "pg_Condominium"]] = [0, 1]
db_scenario.loc[2, "pg_Apartment":"pg_Townhouse"]
```
:::

## Direct and indirect effects, by scenario {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Recompute the lags, predict, compare

The spatial lags must be updated too:

```{python}
wx_scenario = (
    db_scenario.filter(like="pg")
    .apply(lambda y: weights.spatial_lag.lag_spatial(knn, y))
    .rename(columns=lambda c: "w_" + c)
    .drop("w_pg_Apartment", axis=1)
)
slx_exog_scenario = db_scenario[variable_names].join(wx_scenario)
y_pred_scenario = m6.betas[0] + slx_exog_scenario @ m6.betas[1:]
```

Only site 2 and its neighbours can be affected:

```{python}
print(knn.neighbors[2])
```

```{python}
(y_pred_scenario - m6.predy).loc[[2] + knn.neighbors[2]]
```

The first row --- the **direct** effect --- equals the `pg_Condominium` estimate exactly. Every neighbour changes by about $0.03$: the `w_pg_Condominium` estimate divided by the weight of the link, $\frac{1}{20}$.
:::

## Spatial error {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## A spatial lag in the error term

$$\log{P_i} = \alpha + \sum_k \beta_k X_{ki} + u_i, \qquad u_i = \lambda u_{lag-i} + \epsilon_i$$

where $u_{lag-i} = \sum_j w_{i,j} u_j$. This violates the classical OLS assumptions about the error term, so other estimators are needed --- here a generalised method of moments that allows for heteroskedasticity:

```{python}
m7 = spreg.GM_Error_Het(
    db[["log_price"]].values,
    db[variable_names].values,
    w=knn,
    name_y="log_price",
    name_x=variable_names,
)
pandas.DataFrame(
    {
        "Coeff.": m7.betas.flatten(),
        "Std. Error": m7.std_err.flatten(),
        "P-Value": [i[1] for i in m7.z_stat],
    },
    index=m7.name_x,
).reindex(["lambda"]).round(4)
```

The rest of the results read much as before; what is new is an estimate, with inference, for $\lambda$.
:::

## Spatial lag {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## A spatial lag of the dependent variable

$$\log{P_i} = \alpha + \rho \log{P_{lag-i}} + \sum_k \beta_k X_{ki} + \epsilon_i$$

This violates **exogeneity**: $P_i$ appears on both sides of the equation, since it enters the computation of the neighbours' lag. Estimate it with two-stage least squares, using the spatial lags of the explanatory variables as instruments:

```{python}
m8 = spreg.GM_Lag(
    db[["log_price"]].values,
    db[variable_names].values,
    w=knn,
    name_y="log_price",
    name_x=variable_names,
)
pandas.DataFrame(
    {
        "Coeff.": m8.betas.flatten(),
        "Std. Error": m8.std_err.flatten(),
        "P-Value": [i[1] for i in m8.z_stat],
    },
    index=m8.name_z,
).round(4)
```

`W_log_price` applies to all observations and changes the effective strength of every $\beta$. Interpret changes with care --- through predictions and scenarios that separate **direct** and **indirect** components.
:::

# Spatial feature engineering

## What is spatial feature engineering? {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## New information from geographic knowledge

*Spatial feature engineering* develops additional information from raw data using **geographic knowledge**. It happens in two directions:

- **Map matching** --- *between* datasets: geography links samples in separate datasets together.
- **Map synthesis** --- *within* a dataset: geographical structure is used to derive new features from the data already there.
:::

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## A vocabulary

- A **spatial summary feature** measures attributes of observations with some pre-specified spatial relationship to a target observation: the mean or median within a neighbourhood; the **spatial lag**; the count of observations within a distance; the standard deviation of the ten nearest. *Interpolated* features --- transferring information between spatial supports --- also belong here.
- A **proximity feature** measures the distance from a target observation to some other observation or place --- like the distance to Balboa Park in the regression section, or the distance to the nearest other observation.
:::

## Map matching {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Space is the ultimate linkage key

Geographic information is collected at different scales, aggregated with bespoke delineations, and stored in different datasets. Location lets us **connect datasets that share no common key** --- a trick that would be much harder, or impossible, without spatial information.

The difficulty of transferring information between geographies depends on the source, the target, and the precision wanted. There is always a trade-off between **precision and sophistication**: more precise transfer costs more effort, cognitive and computational. Sometimes we need the best estimate at any cost; sometimes "good enough" is good enough.
:::

:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## The cases covered

Counting points of one dataset near points of another; sampling a raster surface at points; attaching polygon attributes to points --- mostly traditional GIS operations. Then two more involved cases: points to points at different locations (interpolation), and polygons to different polygons.
:::

## Counting nearby features {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## How many bars and restaurants near each listing?

```{python}
import rasterio
from rasterio.plot import show as rioshow

airbnbs = geopandas.read_file(f"{GDS}/airbnb/regression_db.geojson")
```

To fetch points of interest from OpenStreetMap we need a polygon covering every listing. The **convex hull** --- the smallest convex polygon containing all the points --- will do:

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
airbnbs_ch = airbnbs.union_all().convex_hull
geopandas.GeoSeries([airbnbs_ch]).plot();
```
:::

## Fetching POIs from OpenStreetMap {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## `osmnx`, restaurants and bars only

The download needs an internet connection:

```python
# Requires internet access -- shown, not run
pois = osmnx.features_from_polygon(
    airbnbs_ch, tags={"amenity": ["restaurant", "bar"]}
).reset_index()
pois = pois.rename(columns=dict(id="osmid"))[
    ["osmid", "amenity", "cuisine", "name", "geometry"]
]
```

A cached copy is in the data folder:

```{python}
pois = geopandas.read_file(f"{GDS}/cache/sd_pois.gpkg")
pois.groupby("amenity").amenity.count()
```

About 1 300 POIs tagged as a restaurant or a bar.
:::

## POIs and listings {.scrollable}

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
f, ax = plt.subplots(1, figsize=(7, 7))
airbnbs.plot(ax=ax, marker=".")
pois.plot(ax=ax, color="r")
contextily.add_basemap(ax, crs=airbnbs.crs.to_string(), source=_carto(contextily.providers.CartoDB.Voyager))
ax.set_axis_off()
plt.show()
```

## Why count them? {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## A "hot" location

A listing in a lively area, with plenty of places to eat and drink, may command higher prices for short city-break stays; a remote one may not. Knowing the dining and drinking scene near each listing might help predict its price. The plan:

1. **Decide what is "nearby"** --- here 500 metres, about a leisurely ten-minute walk.
2. For each listing, find the POIs **within** that distance.
3. **Count** them.
:::

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## First, metres

Both tables are in latitude and longitude:

```{python}
airbnbs.crs
```

```{python}
pois.crs
```

Reproject both to the California Albers projection, in metres:

```{python}
airbnbs_albers = airbnbs.to_crs(epsg=3311)
pois_albers = pois.to_crs(epsg=3311)
pois_albers.crs
```
:::

## Buffer, join, count {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## A 500 m buffer and a spatial join

**Buffering** dilates each point into a circle of the given radius:

```{python}
airbnbs_albers["buffer_500m"] = airbnbs_albers.buffer(500)
```

A **spatial join** links geometries through a spatial predicate --- here, POIs `within` a listing's buffer. Predicates are not always reversible: no buffer can be `within` a POI.

```{python}
joined = geopandas.sjoin(
    pois_albers,
    airbnbs_albers.set_geometry("buffer_500m")[["id", "buffer_500m"]],
    predicate="within",
)
```

Every row is a linked POI-listing pair. Group by listing and count:

```{python}
poi_count = joined.groupby("id")["osmid"].count().to_frame("poi_count")
poi_count.head()
```
:::

## How well served are the listings? {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Back onto the listings

Listings missing from `poi_count` have no POI within 500 m, so their count is zero:

```{python}
airbnbs_w_counts = airbnbs_albers.merge(
    poi_count, left_on="id", right_index=True, how="left"
).fillna({"poi_count": 0})
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
f, ax = plt.subplots(1, figsize=(6, 6))
airbnbs_w_counts.plot(column="poi_count", scheme="quantiles", alpha=0.5, legend=True, ax=ax)
contextily.add_basemap(ax, crs=airbnbs_albers.crs.to_string(), source=_carto(contextily.providers.CartoDB.Voyager))
ax.set_axis_off();
```
:::

## Assigning point values from surfaces {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## What is the elevation of each listing?

A related challenge: transfer the value of a **surface** at a point to a point in another dataset. Needed: the listings, and an elevation surface --- the NASA DEM for the San Diego area.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
dem = rasterio.open(f"{GDS}/nasadem/nasadem_sd.tif")
f, ax = plt.subplots()
rioshow(dem, ax=ax)
ax.set_axis_off();
```

Check the CRS matches the listings:

```{python}
print(dem.crs)
```
:::

## Sampling the surface {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## `dem.sample`

`rasterio` has not read the whole file --- only requested data is loaded, so this works on very large rasters. For one location:

```{python}
list(dem.sample([(-117.24592208862305, 32.761619109301606)]))
```

For all listings, extract their coordinates and sample:

```{python}
abb_xys = pandas.DataFrame(
    {"X": airbnbs.geometry.x, "Y": airbnbs.geometry.y}
).to_records(index=False)

elevation = pandas.DataFrame(
    dem.sample(abb_xys),
    columns=["Elevation"],
    index=airbnbs.index,
)
elevation.head()
```
:::

## Elevation of the listings {.scrollable}

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
f, ax = plt.subplots(1, figsize=(6, 6))
airbnbs.join(elevation).plot(
    column="Elevation", scheme="quantiles", legend=True, alpha=0.5, ax=ax
)
contextily.add_basemap(
    ax, crs=airbnbs.crs.to_string(), source=contextily.providers.Esri.WorldTerrain, alpha=0.5
)
ax.set_axis_off();
```

## Point interpolation {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## When there is no surface

Sometimes all we have are measurements at points that are **not** the points we want. **Spatial interpolation** estimates the value a continuous field takes at unmeasured sites.

Sophisticated options include **kriging** (geostatistics, based on Gaussian process regression) and **geographically weighted regression**. Here, a basic $k$-nearest-neighbour regressor from `scikit-learn`: predict at a site from a distance-weighted average of the nearest ten listings.
:::

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Two-bedroom entire homes only

To keep predictions comparable, interpolate only entire homes with two bedrooms:

```{python}
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor

two_bed_homes = airbnbs[
    (airbnbs["bedrooms"] == 2) & (airbnbs["rt_Entire_home/apt"] == 1)
]
two_bed_home_locations = numpy.column_stack(
    (two_bed_homes.geometry.x, two_bed_homes.geometry.y)
)
len(two_bed_homes)
```
:::

:::{.callout-warning icon=false}
## A correction to the book's filter

The book writes `airbnbs["bedrooms"] == 2 & airbnbs["rt_Entire_home/apt"]`. In Python `&` binds tighter than `==`, so that compares bedrooms with `2 & (0 or 1)`, which is always 0 --- it selects the 445 listings with **zero** bedrooms. Parenthesising each condition selects the intended 1 263.
:::

## A grid to predict on {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## `numpy.meshgrid`

```{python}
xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax = airbnbs.total_bounds
x, y = numpy.meshgrid(numpy.linspace(xmin, xmax), numpy.linspace(ymin, ymax))
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
f, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2)
ax[0].imshow(x)
ax[1].imshow(y)
ax[0].set_title("X values")
ax[1].set_title("Y values")
plt.show()
```

`meshgrid` builds every combination of the input coordinates. Flatten them into prediction points:

```{python}
grid = numpy.column_stack((x.flatten(), y.flatten()))
grid_df = geopandas.GeoDataFrame(
    geometry=geopandas.points_from_xy(x=x.flatten(), y=y.flatten())
)
```
:::

## The grid and the homes {.scrollable}

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
ax = grid_df.plot(markersize=1)
two_bed_homes.plot(ax=ax, color="red")
contextily.add_basemap(
    ax, crs="EPSG:4326", source=_carto(contextily.providers.CartoDB.VoyagerNoLabels)
)
ax.set_axis_off();
```

## Interpolating price {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Train, then predict on the grid

```{python}
model = KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=10, weights="distance").fit(
    two_bed_home_locations, two_bed_homes.price
)
predictions = model.predict(grid)
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
ax = grid_df.plot(predictions)
ax.set_axis_off();
```
:::

## The algorithm shapes the surface {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## More neighbours, smoother surface

The map reflects the algorithm as well as the data:

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
f, ax = plt.subplots(1, 8, figsize=(16, 4))
for i, k_neighbors in enumerate(numpy.geomspace(2, 100, 8).astype(int)):
    facet = ax[i]
    predictions = (
        KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=k_neighbors, weights="distance")
        .fit(two_bed_home_locations, two_bed_homes.price)
        .predict(grid)
    )
    grid_df.plot(predictions, ax=facet)
    facet.axis("off")
    facet.set_title(f"{k_neighbors} neighbors")
```
:::

## Zooming into central San Diego {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## The same, for a smaller area

```{python}
central_sd_bounds = [-117.179832, 32.655563, -117.020874, 32.769909]
central_xmin, central_ymin, central_xmax, central_ymax = central_sd_bounds
central_x, central_y = numpy.meshgrid(
    numpy.linspace(central_xmin, central_xmax),
    numpy.linspace(central_ymin, central_ymax),
)
central_grid = numpy.column_stack((central_x.flatten(), central_y.flatten()))
central_grid_df = geopandas.GeoDataFrame(
    geometry=geopandas.points_from_xy(x=central_x.flatten(), y=central_y.flatten())
)
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
f, ax = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(16, 4), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for i, k_neighbors in enumerate(numpy.geomspace(2, 100, 5).astype(int)):
    facet = ax[i]
    predictions = (
        KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=k_neighbors, weights="distance")
        .fit(two_bed_home_locations, two_bed_homes.price)
        .predict(central_grid)
    )
    central_grid_df.plot(predictions, ax=facet)
    facet.axis("off")
    facet.set_title(f"{k_neighbors} neighbors")
```

More neighbours, smoother surface. More methods live in `sklearn.neighbors`; kriging in `GSTools`; geographically weighted regression in `mgwr`.
:::

## Polygon to point {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Census tract population density for each listing

Find the polygon containing each point and join --- a *spatial join*. Population by tract from the American Community Survey:

```python
# Requires internet access and cenpy -- shown, not run
acs = cenpy.products.ACS()
sd_pop = acs.from_msa("San Diego, CA", level="tract", variables=["B02001_001E"])
```

The cached copy:

```{python}
sd_pop = geopandas.read_file(f"{GDS}/cache/sd_census.gpkg")
sd_pop["density"] = sd_pop["B02001_001E"] / sd_pop.to_crs(epsg=3311).area
```

```{python}
j = geopandas.sjoin(airbnbs, sd_pop.to_crs(airbnbs.crs))
j.info()
```

One row per listing, with the attributes of its tract appended.
:::

## Area to area interpolation {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Different polygons, shared geography

Moving information between two **different areal geographies** is the subject of **dasymetric mapping**. The simplest version apportions values by **shared area**.

Suppose source polygons 1, 2, 3 have population rates, and target polygon A intersects them in 50%, 30% and 20% of its area. A's estimate is the weighted average of the three rates, with weights 0.5, 0.3, 0.2.

The other direction: if A had a total population and 1, 2, 3 did not, allocate A's population **50 / 30 / 20** among them --- assuming A is fully covered by 1, 2, 3 and they do not overlap.

Underneath is the assumption that values are **uniformly distributed** within each polygon. Sometimes acceptable, sometimes not; dasymetric methods add ancillary information to do better.
:::

## `tobler` {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Census tracts to H3 hexagons

The target geography is a grid from the H3 hexagonal index:

```{python}
from tobler.area_weighted import area_interpolate

h3 = geopandas.read_file(f"{GDS}/h3_grid/sd_h3_grid.gpkg")

interpolated = area_interpolate(
    source_df=sd_pop.to_crs(epsg=3311),
    target_df=h3.to_crs(epsg=3311),
    extensive_variables=["B02001_001E"],
    intensive_variables=["density"],
)
```

- Both layers are projected to **California Albers** (`EPSG:3311`, metres), since apportioning by area needs accurate areas.
- **Extensive** variables are absolute values --- counts, totals --- such as population.
- **Intensive** variables are rates and ratios --- such as density.
:::

## Interpolated population {.scrollable}

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
f, axs = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 5))
minX, minY, maxX, maxY = interpolated.total_bounds
sd_pop.to_crs(epsg=3311).cx[minX:maxX, minY:maxY].plot(
    column="B02001_001E", scheme="quantiles", k=10, ax=axs[0]
)
axs[0].set_axis_off()
h3.to_crs(epsg=3311).plot(ax=axs[1], markersize=0.5)
axs[1].set_axis_off()
interpolated.plot(column="B02001_001E", scheme="quantiles", k=10, ax=axs[2])
axs[2].set_axis_off()
axs[0].set_xlim(minX, maxX)
axs[0].set_ylim(minY, maxY)
plt.show()
```

Tracts (left), the hexagon grid (centre), and total population transferred to the hexagons (right).

## Interpolated density {.scrollable}

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
f, axs = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 5))
minX, minY, maxX, maxY = interpolated.total_bounds
sd_pop.to_crs(epsg=3311).cx[minX:maxX, minY:maxY].plot(
    column="density", scheme="quantiles", k=10, ax=axs[0]
)
axs[0].set_axis_off()
h3.to_crs(epsg=3311).plot(ax=axs[1], markersize=0.5)
axs[1].set_axis_off()
interpolated.plot(column="density", scheme="quantiles", k=10, ax=axs[2])
axs[2].set_axis_off()
axs[0].set_xlim(minX, maxX)
axs[0].set_ylim(minY, maxY)
plt.show()
```

The same transfer for population density, an intensive variable.

## Map synthesis {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Features from the data you already have

Map matching shines when there is extra data to bring in. But it is also useful to use the **spatial structure within** your own data to build better features --- without spatially explicit models.

There are many map-synthesis features, often built for specific use cases from domain intuition. Two illustrations: spatial **summary** features, and **regionalization** features --- geographical clusters used as predictors.
:::

## Counting neighbours {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Is a listing surrounded by others?

"Surrounded by other observations" can mean "having many neighbours" --- the **cardinalities** of a spatial weights matrix. Count the listings within 500 m of each listing:

```{python}
d500_w = weights.DistanceBand.from_dataframe(
    airbnbs_albers, threshold=500, silence_warnings=True
)
card = pandas.Series(d500_w.cardinalities)
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
f, ax = plt.subplots(1)
airbnbs.assign(card=card).plot("card", scheme="quantiles", k=7, markersize=1, ax=ax)
contextily.add_basemap(ax, crs=airbnbs.crs, source=BASEMAP)
ax.set_axis_off();
```

Higher values pick up areas of higher concentration of listings.
:::

## Distance buffers within a single table {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## The average size of nearby listings

Row-standardise the 500 m distance band and take the spatial lag of the number of bedrooms:

```{python}
d500_w.transform = "r"
local_average_bedrooms = weights.lag_spatial(d500_w, airbnbs_albers[["bedrooms"]].values)
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
plt.scatter(airbnbs_albers[["bedrooms"]].values, local_average_bedrooms)
plt.xlabel("Number of bedrooms")
plt.ylabel("Average of nearby\n listings' bedrooms");
```

Related, but distinct pieces of information --- both may be useful in a model.
:::

## The most common nearby size {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## `lag_categorical`

For the most common value rather than the average, treat each value as a category:

```{python}
local_mode = weights.lag_categorical(d500_w, airbnbs_albers[["bedrooms"]].values)
crosstab = pandas.crosstab(airbnbs_albers.bedrooms, local_mode.flatten())
crosstab.columns.name = "nearby"
crosstab
```

By far the most common case is a one-bedroom listing surrounded mostly by other one-bedroom listings. The two ten-bedroom properties are also surrounded mostly by one-bedroom listings.
:::

## Summaries from the adjacency list {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Any statistic, via a `groupby`

For more complicated statistics, use the **adjacency list** --- one row per link, with `focal`, `neighbor` and `weight`:

```{python}
adjlist = d500_w.to_adjlist()
adjlist.head()
```

Attach each neighbour's value:

```{python}
adjlist = adjlist.merge(
    airbnbs_albers[["bedrooms"]], left_on="neighbor", right_index=True, how="left"
)
adjlist.head()
```

Then group by the focal observation --- here, the median number of bedrooms around each listing:

```{python}
adjlist.groupby("focal").bedrooms.median()
```

Since the mean and mode are the most common summaries, `lag_spatial` and `lag_categorical` cover most practical needs.
:::

## Ring buffer features {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Further than 500 m, but within 1 km

A **ring buffer** (annulus) summarises observations only within a range of distances. The average within 500 m:

```{python}
average_within_500 = weights.lag_spatial(d500_w, airbnbs_albers[["bedrooms"]].values)
```

The graph of listings within 1 km, minus the links within 500 m:

```{python}
d1k_w = weights.DistanceBand.from_dataframe(airbnbs_albers, threshold=1000, silence_warnings=True)
d1k_exclusive = weights.set_operations.w_difference(d1k_w, d500_w, constrained=False)
d1k_exclusive.transform = "r"
average_500m_to_1k = weights.lag_spatial(d1k_exclusive, airbnbs_albers[["bedrooms"]].values)
```
:::

## Two rings compared {.scrollable}

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
plt.scatter(average_within_500, average_500m_to_1k, color="k", marker=".")
plt.xlabel("Average size within 500 meters")
plt.ylabel("Average size\n beyond 500m but within 1km")
plt.plot([0, 5], [0, 5], color="orangered", linestyle=":", linewidth=2, label="1 to 1")
plt.legend();
```

:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## Related, not the same

The relationship is positive, but with plenty of departure from the line of equality: points above it have larger listings in the 500 m--1 km ring than within 500 m, points below smaller ones.
:::

## Clustering as feature engineering {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Cluster labels as a feature

Clustering can tell us whether an observation is in a particular "place", or is a particular "kind" of observation --- compressing many variables into one categorical feature. That is especially useful when **location** itself says something about the kind of observation found there.

To cluster listings by location, use **HDBSCAN**, a hierarchical variant of DBSCAN from Geo 6. It needs only one parameter: the minimum number of observations in a cluster --- here 25.

```{python}
from sklearn.cluster import HDBSCAN

coordinates = numpy.column_stack((airbnbs_albers.geometry.x, airbnbs_albers.geometry.y))
labels = HDBSCAN(min_cluster_size=25).fit(coordinates).labels_
```

The labels are memberships, not shapes. The convex hull of each cluster's members gives it a geography:

```{python}
hulls = airbnbs_albers[["geometry"]].dissolve(by=labels).convex_hull
```
:::

## Enclaves of listings {.scrollable}

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
f, ax = plt.subplots(1, figsize=(7, 7))
airbnbs_albers.plot(
    column=labels, categorical=True, alpha=0.5, legend=True, ax=ax, marker=".",
    legend_kwds={"bbox_to_anchor": (1, 1), "fontsize": 6},
)
hulls[hulls.index != -1].boundary.plot(color="k", ax=ax)
contextily.add_basemap(
    ax, crs=airbnbs_albers.crs.to_string(),
    source=_carto(contextily.providers.CartoDB.VoyagerNoLabels),
)
ax.set_axis_off();
```

:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## An intermediate scale

The hulls sit between single listings and San Diego as a whole. People choose hierarchically --- the city, then a part of it, then a house --- so these enclaves may carry real information. HDBSCAN picks density thresholds **locally**, so some clusters are less dense than parts of the centre that belong to no cluster.
:::

## Clusters and price {.scrollable}

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
f = plt.figure(figsize=(8, 3))
ax = airbnbs_albers.assign(labels=labels).boxplot(
    "price", by="labels", flierprops=dict(marker=None), ax=plt.gca(),
)
ax.set_xlabel("HDBSCAN cluster")
ax.set_ylabel("price ($)")
plt.gcf().suptitle(None)
ax.set_title(None)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1250);
```

The clusters capture some of the variation in price. To use it in a regression, the labels could serve as the basis for **spatial fixed effects**, as in the previous section.

## Spatial feature engineering: conclusion {.scrollable}

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Enriching data with geography

Feature engineering is within reach whether or not you have auxiliary data. At minimum it builds new variables from existing ones (**map synthesis**); with more data, location is the **ultimate linkage key** that connects datasets with no obvious relationship (**map matching**).

Each operation --- the average near each observation, membership of a cluster --- is simple. Combined, they build large, rich datasets usable in any existing method. The regression and clustering techniques of the previous sections use spatial structure *during* learning; the techniques here put it *into the data*, making non-spatial models geography-aware.
:::
